conversation_lines.text: Did it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were awake, but it shouldn’t have been painful—just some pressure. You tolerated it well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t remember much. I must’ve been out of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar was low this morning—51. We adjusted your insulin sliding scale to prevent more lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having those lately. Thanks for catching it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain is improving, and your vitals are stable. We’re switching from IV to intraperitoneal antibiotics—vancomycin and ceftazidime—so they go directly into the belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’ll get the antibiotics through my catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s more targeted and usually has fewer side effects than IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll do this at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’ll do a 6-hour dwell with the antibiotics after your nightly dialysis. We’ll give you supplies and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if I have another reaction?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. If you develop fever, rash, or trouble breathing, stop and call your nurse or husband immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest peritoneal fluid culture came back—no growth. That’s good. It means the infection might be clearing, though we’ll still finish the full course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: None grew in the lab. Sometimes that happens with peritonitis—we treat based on symptoms and fluid counts even if we don’t find the bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad it’s responding. My belly feels less tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down to 4.6—perfect. That means your body is calming down from the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Does this mean I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly tomorrow. We’ll check one more set of labs and make sure you’re stable. You’ll need to finish 14 days of antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with the antibiotics, but my husband can do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll need to be trained. A nurse will go over the steps with both of you before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gram stain from your fluid today showed a few white cells but no bacteria. That’s expected at this stage—good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The infection markers are improving, and you feel better. That’s what matters most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to come back for follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your nephrologist and primary care. They’ll check your dialysis and make sure the infection doesn’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the intraperitoneal vancomycin and ceftazidime daily for 12 more days. Do a 6-hour dwell after your nightly dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your usual medications—insulin, thyroid, nausea meds, everything. We added lactulose in case you get constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if the pain returns, or if you have fever, cloudy dialysis fluid, or trouble with the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll see my doctors next week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, follow up with your nephrologist and primary care in 7–10 days. We’ll send them all the details.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart my old antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. We’ll discuss prophylaxis with your nephrologist. For now, focus on finishing this course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will go over discharge papers and supplies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in tonight. You had left-sided abdominal pain again, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started this morning—sharp pain in my lower left side. It hasn’t gone away. I was just discharged a few days ago for peritonitis, but this feels different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been doing your antibiotics at home—vancomycin and ceftazidime through your dialysis catheter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did the first one myself last night. A nurse helped before. But the pain never really got better, even with the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We checked your peritoneal fluid today, and the white blood cell count was high—730—so that suggests the infection might still be active.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the cultures were negative last time. Does that mean it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not necessarily. Sometimes we don’t grow anything even when there’s an infection. We’re keeping you on the same antibiotics for now to make sure we treat it fully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also had terrible drain pain last time—so bad I stopped the dwell early. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not typical. We’ll adjust how we do the dwell to make it more comfortable. We gave you some Dilaudid earlier for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also feel nauseated and had diarrhea today. And I’ve had a migraine all evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you Zofran for the nausea. The diarrhea could be from the antibiotics or your gastroparesis acting up. We’ll check your blood sugar and keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach has been slow to empty lately. I’m still a bit constipated too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start a bowel regimen to help with that. Your CT scan didn’t show diverticulitis or any other serious issue—just changes related to your dialysis catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not something else in my intestines?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, the scan looks clear. The fluid and small air pockets are likely from your catheter use over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your peritoneal fluid gram stain showed white blood cells but no bacteria. Cultures are still negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So still no cause?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But the white cells mean inflammation is still there. We’re going to irrigate your peritoneal cavity today to help clear it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s done through your catheter with dialysate fluid. You might feel some fullness or cramping, but we’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The irrigation went well. You tolerated it without complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel some pressure, but it wasn’t too bad. My pain feels a little less intense now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’re also checking for fungal infection just in case, so we started fluconazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fungal? Could that be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s rare, but possible, especially with repeated antibiotics. We’ll stop the fluconazole if the culture comes back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your fungal culture came back negative, so we’re stopping fluconazole. No growth in any cultures so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s still likely bacterial, just not showing up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Or it could be inflammation from the catheter itself. But we’re continuing antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar has been high. I’m worried about my diabetes control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve adjusted your insulin. You’re now on glargine twice daily and a sliding scale. The endocrine team reviewed your regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat peritoneal fluid showed only 14 white blood cells—much better. That suggests the infection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Does that mean I can stop antibiotics soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll likely continue for the full course. You’re on day 8, so two more days. Then we’ll reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gastroparesis? I’m still feeling full quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We restarted Reglan, but we’re watching your EKG for QTc changes. You’re also on domperidone. We’ll keep the bowel regimen going.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal exam is much better today—soft, no tenderness. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better. The pain is almost gone. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge in a day or two. You’ll finish your antibiotics at home and follow up with GI for your gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your repeat cultures are negative, including for TB. No fungus or parasites in your stool either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was just a stubborn bacterial infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. Even without a specific organism, the response to antibiotics and improvement in labs support that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve completed 10 days of antibiotics. Your symptoms are resolved, and labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with instructions for your dialysis, including a manual dwell with antibiotics for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do it myself this time. I think I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse check in. Also, hold vancomycin if your trough level is over 25—we’ll test that at your follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my Reglan? Can I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. But we’ll monitor your heart rhythm. Domperidone is also continuing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my migraines? I’ve been using rizatriptan at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart it. We held it here because it wasn’t on formulary, but it’s fine to use at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I was on 7 units at night, now it’s 6 in the morning and 6 at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. The dose was adjusted for better control. Keep using the sliding scale as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on sevelamer now too? What’s that for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps control your phosphate levels, which were rising. Take it with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dextroamphetamine? I stopped it during this stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can restart it as before. It was held at your request during admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you today. Follow up with your nephrologist and gastroenterologist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to do that. And call if the pain comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Also if you have fever, nausea, or trouble with your dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re being discharged home today. Your condition is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m packed and ready. It’s good to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your discharge summary to your doctors. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Drive safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ll schedule it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good evening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’ve been feeling really tired for weeks. I’ve had nausea, vomiting yellow fluid, and some belly pain near my dialysis catheter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had some fevers. My sugars have been okay, around 150, but I’m still not feeling right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also see you mentioned your toe. Can you tell me about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I stubbed my right big toe on the beach about a month ago. It got infected, and the podiatrist cut part of the nail off. I took antibiotics, but it hasn’t healed. It’s red and painful, with yellow discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ll take a look at that. We’re concerned your symptoms could be from an infection in your peritoneal dialysis fluid, so we’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had that before, back in June. I hope it’s not happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll check your peritoneal fluid. We also did a chest X-ray in the ER — it was clear, so no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ve also had a mild cough, but no shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ll monitor that. Your blood pressure and vitals are stable. We gave you fluids and anti-nausea medicine in the ER.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been constipated too — not had a good bowel movement in days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be contributing. With your gastroparesis and diabetes, constipation can make your stomach feel worse and even affect dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve been on domperidone at home. Can I restart that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted domperidone. Because it can affect heart rhythm, we’ll do daily EKGs to monitor your QT interval.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I’ve had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your foot X-ray. No signs of bone infection or fracture. The redness is likely a skin infection around the nail — paronychia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not osteomyelitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not on the X-ray. If it doesn’t improve, we might consider an MRI, but for now, it looks manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Should I be on antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry will trim the nail tomorrow and assess. We’ll start topical treatment first, since you’re on several meds that affect the heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We checked your peritoneal fluid. No bacteria seen, and cultures show no growth. That’s a good sign — likely not a peritonitis episode.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? But I feel so sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your symptoms are real. We think it’s a mix of worsening gastroparesis and possibly a viral stomach bug. Your blood and urine cultures are also negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. My stomach has been slow for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re increasing your bowel medications — adding lactulose and enemas to help clear your system. Less stool can help your stomach empty better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so backed up. I’ll try anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Podiatry trimmed your toenail. There was a little pus, but it’s minor. We’ll keep it clean and use topical treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did they say why the antibiotics didn’t work?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes oral antibiotics don’t penetrate well in these cases. But since it’s not spreading, we’re avoiding more pills to protect your heart rhythm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also irrigated your peritoneal cavity today to flush things out, just to be safe, even though we don’t think it’s infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially when we’re unsure. It helps reduce any inflammation and keeps the catheter working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. Blood sugar is better, and your kidney function is stable. You’re also starting to have bowel movements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a little less bloated. My nausea is better too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We also did a pelvic exam yesterday because you mentioned vaginal burning and discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been bothering me for a month. I’ve taken fluconazole three times already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you another dose. The swab was negative for yeast, but indeterminate for bacterial vaginosis. If symptoms continue, your PCP might treat for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Abdominal pain is much better, and you’re tolerating food. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Monitor for fever, increased belly pain, or cloudy dialysis fluid — those could suggest infection. Keep your toe clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my medications?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue domperidone with meals, pantoprazole twice daily, and your usual insulin. We added lispro for better mealtime control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my duloxetine? I know we talked about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of your kidney function, we recommend slowly reducing it after discharge. It may be contributing to fatigue. Discuss with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll think about it. It helps my mood, but I’ll talk to my psychiatrist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. We’ll send instructions to your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Focus on small, bland meals, keep up with bowel treatments, and follow up with your doctors next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes — especially with your toe, belly, or dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Oh, and we included a prescription for fluconazole — just in case your vaginal symptoms come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, that’s helpful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — keep monitoring your blood sugars. We adjusted your insulin, so watch for lows.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll check them four times a day like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been having really bad nausea and vomiting for weeks. It’s gotten worse, and I couldn’t keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’re on peritoneal dialysis for your kidney disease, correct? Any changes in that routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m on PD. I haven’t changed the schedule, but I’ve been feeling more bloated and my stomach just isn’t moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That fits with your history of gastroparesis. We’re going to run some tests to make sure nothing else is going on. We’ve ordered a CT scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I was also having diarrhea before I came in. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes with gastroparesis, bowel patterns get irregular. We tested your stool and it came back negative for C. diff, so it’s likely not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. Your blood pressure dropped earlier, and you were a bit confused. Do you remember that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I just remember feeling weak and dizzy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a low blood sugar—down to 20. That can cause confusion. We gave you glucose and fluids, and you improved quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh wow. I didn’t realize it was that low. My diabetes has been hard to manage lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with gastroparesis, it’s tough to time insulin with food that’s not moving through predictably. We’ll adjust your insulin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would help. I’ve been scared to eat much at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start you on small sips and see how you tolerate it. We also gave you some erythromycin to help your stomach empty better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve adjusted the dose for your kidney function. It’s short-term to help get things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan came back. No signs of infection or blockage. Your dialysis catheter is in the right place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So it’s just my gastroparesis acting up again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the diarrhea likely contributed to your low blood pressure. We’re continuing IV fluids and monitoring your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been feeling a little better today. Less nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll try advancing your diet slowly. How’s your pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but manageable. I’ve been using the Zofran before meals like before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll keep that available for you. Also, your blood cultures and peritoneal fluid came back clean—no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I don’t need antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We stopped them yesterday since there’s no sign of infection. Your improvement supports that decision.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray and another abdominal X-ray to check your catheter. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any reason to worry about pneumonia or fluid in my lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lungs look clear. No signs of fluid or infection. Your blood pressure has been stable too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried when I got so confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think that was due to the low blood sugar and dehydration. Your labs are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my anemia? My hemoglobin was low last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s still a bit low, but that’s expected with kidney disease. We’ll monitor it as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a peritoneal irrigation yesterday to make sure there was no buildup causing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did it help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It was precautionary. No signs of infection, but it helps clear any debris. You’re tolerating food better now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had some broth and toast this morning. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent progress. We’ll keep building up slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your potassium was low earlier, so we’re giving you supplements. It’s important with your diuretics and dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t realize I was low. Any symptoms I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Muscle cramps or weakness. We’ll check it again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my insulin—what’s the plan there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered your long-acting insulin because your morning sugars were too low. We’ll send you home with a new schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been waking up shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if all goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most of your usual ones. We’re continuing domperidone and lubiprostone. We stopped the erythromycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tizanidine? I’ve been feeling groggy in the mornings.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve lowered it from 12mg to 2mg at night. It wasn’t clearing well with your kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That explains it. I’ll be more alert during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea worsens, try a liquid diet for a few days. Avoid constipation—it makes gastroparesis worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood sugars?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow the new insulin plan. Check your potassium in a few days—we’ve ordered the lab test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, with your PCP, GI, and endocrinology. We’re setting up a gastroparesis specialist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Take it slow, stick to the meds, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.text: Your vitals are stable. Blood pressure 149/84, heart rate 89. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’ll follow all the instructions.

conversation_lines.text: One more thing—avoid driving while taking lorazepam. It can add to drowsiness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, your husband is listed as your contact. He can help monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, he’ll be here soon to pick me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.text: Good luck.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks.

conversation_lines.text: We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I feel safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s what matters.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been so nauseous and vomiting. I haven’t been able to eat. And the nerve pain—burning, stabbing all over my arms and legs—it’s unbearable. I couldn’t sleep at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through that. We saw in your chart you have gastroparesis and diabetic neuropathy. Did you skip your dialysis last night?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I was too sick. I just couldn’t do it. My stomach was so full, and the pain was everywhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll get you started on IV fluids and some anti-nausea meds. Your sodium is low, which could be from not eating or drinking. We’ll watch that closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But please, can I get something for the nerve pain? I’ve tried gabapentin before—it didn’t help. I just need relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Because of your kidney disease, some pain meds aren’t safe. But we can try pregabalin, which works for nerve pain and is safer for you. We’ll start it tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And no narcotics, right? I don’t want to break my contract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct. We won’t use narcotics. We’ll focus on safe, effective options for your neuropathy and fibromyalgia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures and peritoneal fluid came back negative—no infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. I was worried about peritonitis again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We irrigated your peritoneal cavity yesterday to make sure it’s clean. Your PD will continue as planned. How’s the nausea today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better since the IV fluids. But I still feel full and queasy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping you on IV ondansetron for now. We’ll also start erythromycin to help your stomach empty. It’s a motility agent, safe for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. It helped. But I got dizzy with promethazine—should I avoid that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. You had low blood pressure after it, so we stopped it. We’ll stick with ondansetron, which is safer for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your gastric emptying study shows 38% of food still in your stomach after 4 hours. That confirms moderate to severe gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full. Will the erythromycin help long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps short-term. For long-term, GI plans to do an EGD with botox injection after discharge. That can relax the stomach valve and improve emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. What about my pain? The pregabalin helped a little, but I’m still uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added nortriptyline at night. It helps with nerve pain and can improve sleep. We started at 25mg, but lowered it to 10mg because you felt groggy in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that was better. I wasn’t so tired. Is it safe with my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’ll monitor your EKG. Some of your meds, like nortriptyline and fluoxetine, can affect heart rhythm. We’ll check it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You haven’t vomited in over 24 hours—that’s great progress. We’re switching your anti-nausea med to the dissolvable ondansetron tablet, as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t needed it much today. Can I try a small meal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start with something light—like broth or applesauce. We’ll watch how you tolerate it. Your constipation is also improving with your usual laxatives.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that too. What about my insulin? I haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We kept your long-acting insulin the same but reduced your mealtime doses since you’re not eating. We’ll adjust it back as you resume eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs today show your sodium is stable at 130, and kidney function is consistent. Creatinine improved slightly to 4.6.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that good? I know my kidneys aren’t great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable, which is what we want. You’re still on peritoneal dialysis as scheduled. No signs of fluid overload or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain? I’m sleeping better with the nortriptyline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The pregabalin and nortriptyline together are helping. We stopped gabapentin since it wasn’t working and pregabalin is better for your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had no nausea for two days and are tolerating soft foods. We’ll stop the IV meds today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge on Friday. You’ll go home with pregabalin and nortriptyline. Keep using ondansetron as needed for nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my domperidone? I brought it from home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can continue it. It’s not on the official list because it’s not FDA-approved here, but it’s helping your stomach, so keep taking it as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last night you walked to the nursing station without issues. Your strength and balance are good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much stronger. The pain is manageable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discontinue the erythromycin tomorrow morning. You don’t need it long-term. Keep up with your home meds for constipation and reflux.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another gastric study?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not now. The one we did confirmed the diagnosis. The next step is the EGD with botox, which GI will schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my mental health meds? I’ve been taking them all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on fluoxetine, clonazepam, and modafinil—all continued as before. They help with mood, anxiety, and fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. We’re discharging you today. You’ll go home with services to help with follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel so much better. No vomiting, and the pain is under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Remember to follow up with GI, your nephrologist, and your primary doctor. Keep taking your new meds—pregabalin daily and nortriptyline at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And get the EKG checks, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your pharmacist recommended regular EKGs due to the combination of medications. Call us if nausea returns or pain worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. You’re alert, walking well, and your vitals are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will go over your discharge instructions and meds. Your husband can come up now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. You’re cleared to go home. Rest, follow up, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re glad you’re feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’ve been having trouble breathing, especially when I walk or do anything. It’s been getting worse over the past week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any chest pain, fever, or cough?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever or cough. I do feel some tightness in my chest, but not sharp pain. And I fell out of bed a few nights ago—hit my head, but didn’t black out.

conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was worried about that. But why am I so short of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on that. Your chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia or fluid. Your heart enzyme and EKG were normal too, so it’s likely not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been really weak and tired since the fall. And I’ve mostly been drinking water—haven’t been eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Your sodium level is quite low—120 when it should be around 135. That could explain the fatigue and weakness. Given you’re on dialysis and not eating, it’s likely due to poor salt and food intake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s because I’m not eating? But I thought dialysis handled that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Dialysis helps, but you still need some salt and food. Right now, your body isn’t getting enough solutes. We call it ‘tea and toast syndrome.’ We’ll adjust your fluids and continue dialysis to help correct it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve also been constipated—maybe that’s not helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, constipation can make you feel worse. We’ll give you some enemas to help clear things out. We also saw your urine culture showed a bacterial infection—gram-negative rods. Even if you don’t have symptoms, we need to treat it since you’re on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even know I had a UTI. Will the antibiotics be okay with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re using Bactrim, which is dosed carefully for dialysis patients. You’ll take it for 7 days. We’ll check the final sensitivities to make sure it’s effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sodium is up to 126 today—heading in the right direction. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel a little less tired. Did they do that stress test yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was done yesterday. Your heart looked great—normal blood flow, no signs of blockage. That confirms your shortness of breath isn’t from your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. But I still feel weak. And my right hip and leg hurt—has been for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be related to your neuropathy from diabetes. We’ll keep managing your pain with pregabalin and tizanidine. Let us know if it gets worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my stomach—still feels slow. I’m not hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding domperidone to help with your gastroparesis. It helps your stomach empty better. We’ll also keep your usual bowel regimen with senna and lubiprostone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also did an irrigation of your peritoneal cavity today as part of your dialysis. It’s routine to make sure there’s no infection buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is everything looking clean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your dialysis fluid showed no signs of infection—no white cells or bacteria. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show your sodium is now 128, and potassium is improving too. We’re on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I had a headache yesterday—felt like my usual migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned photophobia. You can still use your sumatriptan as needed. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my dry cough and hoarse voice—still there. Is that from the intubation a few weeks ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. Intubation can irritate the throat. We’ve added lozenges for comfort. It should improve over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray tonight. No bowel obstruction. There’s some gas in your colon, but that’s common with constipation and gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing urgent. We’ll keep working on your bowel movements with polyethylene glycol starting tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your sodium is now 130, and you’re breathing better. We think you’re ready to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your usual medications. Take the Bactrim for the full 7 days. Use the new polyethylene glycol daily for constipation. And keep using domperidone with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure—sometimes I feel dizzy when I stand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noticed some orthostatic hypotension. It’s likely from your neuropathy. Stand up slowly. If dizziness continues, your doctor might start midodrine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And when should I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your primary doctor next week. They’ll check your sodium and potassium. Call if you have fever, trouble breathing, or severe pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and keep up with your dialysis and diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—make sure your pharmacy isn’t refilling metoprolol. You shouldn’t be on it. Let your doctor know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know. I’ll check that right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ll also send a note to your care team. You’re doing well—just keep managing your symptoms at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to stay on top of everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll have a nurse go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, if the UTI symptoms develop—like burning or urgency—call your doctor. Otherwise, finish the antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your stress test was completely normal, so no heart issues. That’s a big relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s really good to hear. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally understandable. But all signs point to your symptoms being from the low sodium, poor intake, and the UTI—all of which are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better already. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up the good work at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And how’s your breathing? You mentioned shortness of breath on your chart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it comes and goes. Some days I can walk around the block with my cane, but today I can barely move across the room. I feel so weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Low sodium? But I’ve been drinking tea and eating toast. Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
