conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So it’s not something more serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s serious enough that we need to treat it, but it’s fixable. We’ll restart your dialysis manually and restrict your fluids to 1 liter a day. We’ll also give you some extra nutrients to help raise your sodium safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds doable. What about the bloating and constipation? I’ve been on laxatives, but nothing’s working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CT scan shows a lot of stool in your colon, so you’re definitely constipated. But no blockage, which is good. We’ll start with enemas to help clear it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Enemas? I’ve never done those at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll teach you how. The nursing team will show you how to use a soap suds enema safely. It’s important to keep your bowels moving, especially with your dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll try it. And my potassium is low too, right? I saw that on my last lab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your potassium was 2.6, which is low. We’re giving you supplements, and your dialysis will help balance it. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from this morning show your sodium is up to 122. That’s a good start.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s better, right? How high should it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Normal is around 135, but we’re aiming to get it above 130. We don’t want to raise it too fast, or it could cause other problems. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I did the enema last night. I had a big bowel movement. Felt so much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll keep doing them twice a day for now to make sure you stay regular. The nursing team will help you practice so you can do it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m a little nervous about doing it myself, but I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ll walk you through it step by step. It’s very safe, and it’s important for your health with your dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your peritoneal fluid today to make sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that because of my history of peritonitis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We always check when you’re having abdominal symptoms. The good news is, no bacteria were seen, and the culture came back negative. No sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We were too. We also irrigated your peritoneal cavity today with dialysate to help clear any buildup and make dialysis more effective.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did that hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You were awake, but it’s usually well tolerated. It helps keep the catheter working well and prevents complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your sodium is now 124, and potassium is 2.9. Both are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good! I feel a bit stronger today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to keep the fluid restriction and continue the enemas. The nephrology team also said to stop your furosemide—it’s not needed since you’re on dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I was taking that for swelling, but I haven’t had any lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Dialysis handles that now. We’ll keep you on all your other meds, like domperidone for gastroparesis and your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, can I ask about my green stool? Is that from the enema?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Sometimes enemas or changes in bowel motility can alter stool color. Since you’re moving your bowels now and feel better, it’s likely not a concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, just wanted to make sure it wasn’t infection or something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we ruled that out. Your peritoneal fluid was clean, and your white count is normal. No signs of infection anywhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your sodium is now 126, and urea and creatinine are down. Your dialysis is working well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might be able to go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if things keep improving. We’ll plan for discharge tomorrow. But you’ll need to keep up with the enemas at home and stay on your 1-liter fluid limit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And go back to my regular dialysis cycler?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Back to your usual schedule. And please follow up with your nephrologist and GI doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, I’ve been thinking—should I change my diet to avoid this low sodium again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Try to include more protein and salt in small amounts—like broth, Nepro supplement, or crackers. When you’re nauseous, it’s easy to fall back on tea and toast, but that’s what got you here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. Maybe I can keep some Nepro on hand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great idea. Your primary doctor will check your sodium in a few days. Please send the results to your nephrologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a few reminders: keep doing your enemas daily, stick to 1 liter of fluids, and restart your regular dialysis cycler.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And call if I start feeling bloated or weak again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep up with your follow-up appointments. You’re doing a great job managing a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what brought you in today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi. I’ve been having bad abdominal pain, headaches, and just overall body pain. I feel really weak and nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The abdominal pain—where exactly is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s in my lower belly, both sides. Not sharp, but constant. And my headaches feel like my usual migraines.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, chest pain, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no fever or chest pain. Just some chills now and then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And how has your eating been?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not good. I’ve only been eating toast. Nauseous a lot, and I’ve been vomiting. Also had green diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And when was your last bowel movement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t remember exactly, but it’s been days. Maybe over a week?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ll check your labs and do an ultrasound to look at your liver and gallbladder since your lipase and alkaline phosphatase were elevated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that tell us what’s wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It helps rule out things like gallstones or pancreatitis. But given your history of gastroparesis and constipation, we’re also concerned about bowel issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was just here two weeks ago for similar problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I saw that. You had hyponatremia then, which improved with dialysis. Your sodium is better now, but we still need to manage your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your ultrasound came back normal—no gallstones or liver issues. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think it’s mostly due to constipation and your gastroparesis. Your abdomen is soft, no signs of infection. We’ll start a stronger bowel regimen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what I use at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, plus we’ll add Miralax and lactulose. If that doesn’t work, we may use a soap suds enema, like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I remember that helped before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed you haven’t had dialysis since before admission. We’d like to do a session tomorrow to help with your overall feeling of malaise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, please. I feel so sluggish.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bloated. Haven’t had a bowel movement yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you a soap suds enema this morning. It should help. Also, your labs show your kidney function is stable, and your glucose is manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for noon today. It should help with your nausea and fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just had a bowel movement! That enema worked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! That should help your abdominal pain. How’s your headache?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I took my sumatriptan yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. And your leg pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but same as usual. Shooting pains, but no new weakness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds like your fibromyalgia. We’ll keep you on your regular meds for that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How did the dialysis go?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Tiring, but I feel a bit clearer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your labs are improving. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if you keep feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been thinking… I don’t want to be resuscitated if my heart stops. I’ve had enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We can complete a MOLST form to document that. You’d still want hospitalization if needed, but no CPR or intubation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I just don’t want extreme measures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll go over the form with you now so you can sign it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your vitals are stable, and your pain is much improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll send you home with instructions to continue the bowel regimen—Miralax daily, plus your usual meds. And keep up with your peritoneal dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I still use enemas if I get backed up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as needed. And please follow up with your GI doctor soon. This is the second time in a month, so we need to adjust your plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my headaches and body pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your sumatriptan for migraines and your regular fibromyalgia meds. If anything worsens, call your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll have your discharge papers ready soon, including the MOLST form. Take care, and follow up as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the surgery team members. You’re here today for your scheduled pancreas and kidney transplant, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I’ve been waiting for this call for months. Is everything set for surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry, but I have some news. The donor organs were evaluated and unfortunately weren’t suitable for transplant. They didn’t meet the safety or function criteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I was really hoping this would happen. Does that mean I’m not getting the transplant at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not today. You’re still fully listed and active for transplant. This just means we have to wait for another donor match. It’s disappointing, but not uncommon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I guess I just feel let down. I’ve been doing everything right—my PD, my meds, my diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You absolutely have. Your labs look stable—creatinine is high as expected, but no signs of infection or acute issues. Your chest X-ray also looks clear, which is good for surgical clearance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that DNR status on file since last time. Does that affect anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually something we discussed with the team. Since you were admitted for transplant, we temporarily reversed your DNR status for the perioperative period, just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. But since there’s no surgery, does that mean my DNR is back in place?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since no procedure is happening, your current wishes stand. The transplant clinic will follow up with you about the MOLST form and your code status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I just want to be clear about what happens next.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. You’ll go home today. You should continue your peritoneal dialysis as usual and take all your regular medications, including insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on domperidone before—can I restart that? It helps with my gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve added domperidone to your discharge list—10 mg three times a day before meals. It’s safe with your current meds and should help with fullness and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. And if I get sick or something changes, I should call the transplant clinic, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Any hospitalization, illness, or even insurance changes—let them know. It could affect your listing status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. So no surgery today, but I’m still on the list and just waiting for the next call.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. We know it’s frustrating, but your spot hasn’t changed. We’ll keep supporting you until the right match comes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I was nervous coming in, but I feel better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You should be able to go home in the next hour or so.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I monitor my blood sugar more closely now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep checking as usual. Your HbA1c is 6.4%, which is good control. Just stick with your glargine and sliding scale as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my PD—no changes there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No changes. Continue your peritoneal dialysis exactly as you do at home. If you notice any signs of infection around the catheter, call your nephrologist right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for walking me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll be in touch if anything changes. Take care, and we’ll see you when the next opportunity comes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be ready. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. I see you were admitted for nausea and vomiting, but you’ve also been feeling unwell for a while. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve just felt terrible. Everything hurts—my joints, my muscles. I’m so tired, I can’t eat, and I’ve been vomiting. It’s been getting worse for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry you’re going through this. You mentioned pain—where is it the worst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: All over, but my right hip really aches. And I’ve been constipated too. I tried taking extra oxycodone for the pain, but it didn’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. The oxycodone might actually be making the constipation worse. We’ll need to look at that. I also see you’re on peritoneal dialysis. Has that been working okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I’ve been doing longer sessions at night, but I still feel bloated and sick. I even tried one session of hemodialysis, but I got so dizzy and low blood pressure that they stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll stick with peritoneal dialysis for now and monitor your fluid balance closely. We’ve ordered some tests—blood work, a chest X-ray, and we’ll check your dialysis fluid too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the X-ray show anything serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray came back. There’s no pneumonia or fluid in your lungs. Just some mild changes from atelectasis, which is common and not dangerous. So that’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hip pain? Could it be broken?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The imaging shows no fracture. There are some degenerative changes, like arthritis, but nothing acute. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m just so tired of being sick all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’re going to work on getting your symptoms under control. Your labs show low sodium, which could be contributing to your fatigue and nausea. We’ll adjust your fluids carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the dialysis?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Fluid and electrolyte imbalances are common with ESRD. We’ll monitor it closely. Also, your blood cultures came back negative—no infection in the bloodstream.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my dialysis fluid? Could that be infected?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked that too. The first test showed no white blood cells or bacteria. So no signs of peritonitis, which is great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did notice your abdomen X-ray shows some stool buildup. That’s likely why you’re constipated. The oxycodone isn’t helping that. We may need to adjust your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I need something for the pain. It’s constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. We’ll find a balance. For now, we’re going to irrigate your peritoneal cavity to make sure the dialysis is working properly. It’s a quick procedure to clear any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The irrigation was done. It went smoothly. We hope this helps your dialysis work better and reduces your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Do you think I’ll start feeling better soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving in the right direction. We’re also watching your phosphorus levels—they’re a bit off, which is common with kidney disease. We’ll adjust your binders.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat dialysis fluid culture is back—still no growth, no infection. That’s excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure? I’m scared of another drop like with hemodialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping a close eye on it. You’ve had some episodes of low blood pressure, but they’ve been mild. We’re adjusting your fluid removal rate to be safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I also have this chest pain sometimes. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not typical heart pain. Given your history, it could be musculoskeletal or from acid reflux. We’ll keep an eye on it, but no red flags so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your appetite still low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. I feel full quickly, and gastroparesis makes it hard to keep food down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing your domperidone. It helps with stomach emptying. We also see you’re anemic—common with kidney disease. We’ll manage that with your usual treatments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve lost weight too. I feel like I’m failing to thrive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern, and we’re documenting it. We’ll work with nutrition to get you some high-calorie supplements that are dialysis-friendly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. Nausea is less, but I’m still weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. Your sodium is improving, and you’re not retaining as much fluid. We’re slowly backing off some IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re getting there. We want to make sure your pain is managed without over-relying on opioids, and that your dialysis is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another set of blood cultures came back negative. No infection. That’s very good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my urine test?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It showed mixed bacteria, but it’s likely contamination from skin or genital area. Not a real infection, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I don’t want more meds if I don’t need them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another check on your dialysis fluid—still clean. No signs of infection. Your labs are trending in the right direction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my hip pain? It’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely from arthritis and chronic pain syndrome. We’re using Lyrica and non-opioid strategies. We’ll continue physical therapy when you’re stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still anxious and depressed. It’s hard to stay positive.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We haven’t forgotten that. Your mental health is important. We’ve consulted psychology, and they’ll talk to you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all goes smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue peritoneal dialysis as scheduled. Take your insulin, domperidone, and other meds. We’re switching your pain management to avoid high-dose opioids to prevent constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your nephrologist and pain specialist soon. Also, your sleep apnea and migraines need ongoing care. Keep using your CPAP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come back if nausea, vomiting, or pain gets worse. Also watch for fever or cloudy dialysis fluid—those could mean infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve updated all your medications. The constipation was partly from the oxycodone, so we’re reducing that and adding a stool softener.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll stick to the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Keep in touch with your team. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Someone will bring your discharge papers shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to follow up with your primary team and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made good progress. Keep it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That means a lot.
